title.say: Where does Kosovo keep its money?

title: Every year, the central bank publishes the answer. Here is twenty twenty-five.
size: Add up every bank, pension fund, insurer and lender, and you get fourteen point six billion euros.
That is about a third more than the whole economy produces in a year.

size.say: Banks hold two thirds of it.
Microfinance and insurance share the rest.

growth: In twenty twenty-one, the total was under nine billion.
Four years later, it is almost two thirds bigger.

growth.say: Last year alone, it grew by nearly fifteen percent.

banks.say: Start with the banks. There are ten, and seven belong to foreign groups.

banks: People and companies have deposited seven point eight billion euros.
The banks have lent out six point seven billion.
A little more than half goes to businesses. The rest goes to households, and their share keeps rising.
The three largest banks hold more than half of all banking assets.
rates: In December, the average interest rate on loans was six point eight percent.
Savers earned three and a half percent on deposits.

rates.say: The gap between the two widened again.

rates: Banks made a profit of one hundred and eighty-five million euros, the most in at least ten years.
health: About two percent of loans are not being repaid on time.
Banks hold capital worth seventeen percent of their risk-weighted assets.
And they keep almost three times the liquid reserves the rules require.

health.say: In the central bank's stress test, the system held up, even in the severe scenario.

pensions: One fund, the Kosovo Pension Savings Trust, holds almost all of it: three point eight billion euros.

pensions.say: Four fifths of that money is invested abroad.

pensions: In twenty twenty-five, investments earned three hundred and nine million euros,
almost as much as workers paid in.

others.say: Insurance is small. Premiums came to one hundred and seventy-nine million euros.

others: Nearly half of that is compulsory car insurance. Life insurance is under five percent.
Microfinance and other non-bank lenders are growing fastest.

others.say: But their loans cost eighteen percent a year, on average.

payments.say: The way people pay is changing too.

payments: The number of debit cards grew by a third in one year, to almost one point nine million.

payments.say: Card payments in shops rose by a third as well.

payments: More than a million accounts can now be used online.
Instant payments are being built. Joining the Single Euro Payments Area is still waiting on legislation.
outro: Household debt rose by almost a fifth in one year.
The property market leans on money from the diaspora.
And the central bank expects inflation to rise in twenty twenty-six.

outro.say: For now, the numbers describe a system that is small, built around banks, growing fast, and stable.
